extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, lawmakers, and citizens interested in legitimacy of government
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria for when political power, conquest, usurpation, tyranny, resistance, and governmental dissolution are lawful or unlawful according to classical political theory. Focuses on origins of authority (consent, law), limits on rulers, and justifications for resistance or re-constitution of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest does not confer title to dispossess posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: No damage that men in the state of nature suffer from one another can give a conqueror power to dispossess the posterity of the vanquished and turn them out of their inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that the losses inflicted by war (destruction of a few years' product, seizure of treasure) rarely equal the perpetual value of land, and thus 'the satisfying of what shall, on this score, be due to the conqueror, will scarce give him a title to any country he shall conquer.' A conqueror's power is at best bare force, not a lawful title extending to descendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extorted promises are not valid consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises or promises extorted by force cannot be thought consent and 'they bind not at all'; what is obtained by force does not obligate the victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: a thief who takes a purse at pistol-point or forces a promise has not created a lawful obligation. The law of nature obliges only by voluntary adherence to its rules, not by coerced acts; thus obligations obtained under force are void and may be resumed by the injured party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children of the conquered remain free
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute power of the conqueror reaches no farther than the persons of the men that were subdued by him, and dies with them; it cannot lawfully extend to their children who are in their minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since a father has not power over the life or liberty of his child, no act of his can forfeit it; descendants retain their natural freedom and cannot be born into lawful subjection because of their ancestors' defeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural double right: bodily liberty and inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is born with a double right: (1) a right of freedom to his person; (2) a prior right to inherit his father's goods with his brethren.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two natural rights ground Locke's claims about freedom from arbitrary subjection and the protection of property; they frame evaluations of any authority that attempts to override personal liberty or hereditary property without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renunciation of lawful government requires forfeiture of its derived rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man disclaims the lawful government of the country he was born in, he must also quit rights that belonged to him by the laws of it and the possessions descending from it, if it was a government made by consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notes a corollary: consenting to leave a government's protection or lawfully renouncing membership implies giving up attendant legal claims that depended on that government's consented order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descendants retain property rights despite ancestors' forced submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Inhabitants descended from those who were subdued and had a government forced upon them retain a right to the possessions of their ancestors, even if they do not freely consent to their current government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the first conqueror never had a right to the land, descendants may 'shake off' usurpation or tyranny and reclaim rightful government when they can freely choose or have laws to which they or their representatives have given free consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants by conqueror become property and cannot be arbitrarily revoked
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conqueror grants estates or tenures, those grants create property interests which cannot be taken away without the grantee's consent; otherwise contracts and voluntary conveyances become void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke asks rhetorically whether a grant 'to him and his heirs for ever' could be revoked by the grantor's power. He uses this to show that arbitrary revocation would make all voluntary contracts illusory and destroy property security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers are bound by the laws of God and nature; oaths and promises bind even omnipotence
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes owe subjection to the laws of God and nature; grants, promises, and oaths are bonds that hold the Almighty, and no power can exempt anyone from these obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative limit on sovereign authority: even a monarch's prerogative cannot free him from moral and natural-law obligations, so claims of absolute exemption from law are illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited rights of conqueror: power over actual participants and compensation for damage
rubrics_metrics.description: A conqueror, if he have a just cause, has a despotical right over those who actually aided or concurred in the war and may make up his damage and cost out of their labour and estates, so long as he injures not the right of any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even this limited right does not extend to arbitrary dominion over a whole people or their posterity; Locke distinguishes between recompense for harms and claiming sovereign title over an entire nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usurpation lacks rightful claim until popular consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever gets into the exercise of power by other ways than what the laws of the community have prescribed hath no right to be obeyed; an usurper cannot have a title until the people are both at liberty to consent and have actually consented to confirm him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usurpation is a change of persons without lawful change of government form; obedience is owed only to lawful, law-prescribed designations of rulers or those subsequently consented to by the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny defined: exercise of power beyond right for private ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny is the exercise of power beyond right, used not for the good of those under it but for the ruler's private advantage; when the governor makes his will the rule rather than the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke contrasts a rightful king who seeks the public good and obeys fundamental laws with a tyrant who rules for 'ambition, revenge, covetousness, or any other irregular passion.' Any form of government can become tyrannical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where law ends, tyranny begins; unlawful acts may be opposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever in authority exceeds the power given him by law and harms another thereby ceases to be a magistrate and may be opposed like any other man who by force invades another's right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle applies to magistrates at all levels: exceeding lawful authority nullifies official protection and makes resistance lawful against acts that transgress law to another's harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force is to be opposed only when it is unjust and unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: Force should be opposed only to unjust and unlawful force; opposition in other cases draws just condemnation and endangers polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes restraint: legitimate resistance is not a license for private grievance-based rebellion but is limited to resisting actual unlawful force (e.g., self-defense when life is threatened).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force warranted when legal remedies are unavailable or untimely
rubrics_metrics.description: Force is only to be used where it leaves not the remedy of such an appeal to the law; unjust force that prevents an appeal to law puts the injured in a state of war and justifies resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: killing a highway robber threatening life is lawful because legal recourse is too late to save life; but use of force to recover stolen money when legal remedy exists is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch's person may be legally privileged, but unlawful acts by agents remain resistible
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries the person of the prince is sacred and cannot be subjected to violence, but unlawful acts by inferior officers executed under royal commission, when beyond legal limits, may be opposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sacredness of the monarch's person does not validate illegal acts committed by agents; commissions cannot empower actions that contravene the law's inherent limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective resistance justified when unlawful acts are widespread or threaten all
rubrics_metrics.description: If illegal acts extend to a majority, or seem likely to threaten the laws, estates, liberties, lives, or religion of all, the people are justified in resisting unlawful force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that isolated injustices will not usually provoke general revolt, but systematic or credible threats to the whole society remove practical and moral obstacles to collective resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of arbitrariness and sustained experiments in arbitrary power justify alarm
rubrics_metrics.description: A long train of actions showing councils tending toward arbitrary power, favouring operators who introduce it, and steady experiments of arbitrary authority are legitimate grounds for public suspicion and eventual resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke urges attention to cumulative signs—repeated infringements, supported agents, and covert establishment of contrary religion—as indicia that government is tending toward tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: External conquest dissolves society and thus its government
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual way society is dissolved is the inroad of foreign force making a conquest upon them; when the society is dissolved the government cannot remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conquest that scatters the body politic effectively ends the union that constituted the commonwealth; the frame (government) cannot subsist if its material (people/society) is dissipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration or dissolution of the lawful legislative dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislative is broken or dissolved, dissolution and death of the commonwealth follows; the legislative is the soul that declares the public will and keeps the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If persons make laws without authorization or the legislative's freedom to deliberate is removed, those actions change the legislative and dissolve the government's legitimate authority, permitting resistance and reconstitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince substituting his will for law alters the legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single person sets up his own arbitrary will in place of the laws which are the will of the society, the legislative is changed and his acts set up a new legislative without authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes introducing new laws or subverting old ones without the fundamentals or appointment of the society; such substitution of will for law is central to dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing legislature from assembling or acting freely dissolves it
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prince hinders the legislative from assembling in its due time, or from acting freely (debating and perfecting what is for the good of the society), the legislative is altered and the government dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke stresses that mere names or meetings do not constitute government; the functional freedom to exercise legislative power is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering electors or methods of election without consent dissolves the legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by arbitrary power, the electors or ways of election are altered without consent and contrary to the common interest, the legislative is altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing who chooses legislators or how they are chosen undermines the people's delegated authority and can justify reconstitution of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of the people into subjection to a foreign power dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: The delivery of the people into the subjection of a foreign power, either by the prince or the legislative, is certainly a change of the legislative and a dissolution of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because entering society aimed at preserving independence and self-government, giving up that independence to another power breaches the social compact and dissolves legitimate governmental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect or abandonment by the executive of law-execution dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: When he who has the supreme executive power neglects and abandons that charge so that the laws already made can no longer be put in execution, the government is demonstratively reduced to anarchy and dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The administration of justice and execution of laws are the bonds of society; without execution, laws are ineffectual and the government effectively ceases to exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's right to erect a new legislative when government dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government is dissolved by the alterations above, the people are at liberty to provide for themselves by erecting a new legislative differing in persons or form as shall be most for their safety and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes the people's original and continuing right to preserve themselves: dissolution by another does not forfeit the society's right to reconstitute legitimate authority, though realistic constraints (timeliness, capacity) may apply.
